pages.name: A steady push
pages.text: Gas at a steady 200 kPa, an example, pushes a piston out, and its volume grows from 0.1 to 0.3 m³. Work is the push times the distance moved. The push is the pressure times the piston’s area, and that area times the distance is the volume swept, so the work is the pressure times the [[change in volume]]. On a [[pV diagram]], pressure up the side and volume along the bottom, that is the rectangle under the flat line: 200 × 0.2 = 40 kJ. A kPa is a kN on each m², so a kPa times a m³ is a kN m, a kJ.

pages.name: A steady 300 kPa
pages.task: Gas at a steady 300 kPa, an example, pushes the piston out from 0.05 m³ to 0.15 m³. How much work does it do?
pages.why: The work is the pressure times the change in volume: 0.15 − 0.05 = 0.1 m³, so 300 × 0.1 = 30 kJ, the rectangle under the flat line. 300 × 0.15 = 45 kJ counts the 0.05 m³ the gas filled before the piston moved. 300 × 0.05 = 15 kJ uses the start volume, not the change.

pages.name: Bars under a curve
pages.text: Usually the pressure falls as the gas expands: the same gas spread through more room presses less on each square metre. Here it follows `pV² = C`, an example. 400 kPa in 0.1 m³ makes `C` = 400 × 0.1² = 4, so at 0.2 m³ the pressure is 4 ÷ 0.2² = 100 kPa. No one rectangle fits, so cut the change in volume into bars, each as tall as the pressure at its middle: the [[mid-ordinate rule]]. Each bar is a pressure times a change in volume, a little work. Four bars give 19.82 kJ, eight 19.95 kJ and a hundred 20.00 kJ.
pages.alt: Pressure falling along pV squared equals 4. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.2 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 20.00 kJ. 100 bars, each 0.1 divided by 100 equals 0.001 cubic metres wide. Each: the pressure at its middle times its width. 100 bars: 20.00 kJ, settled on 20 kJ

pages.name: One bar
pages.task: Cut the stretch from 0.1 to 0.2 m³ into two bars. The first runs from 0.1 to 0.15 m³; its middle is at 0.125 m³, where the pressure is 4 ÷ 0.125² = 256 kPa. How much work does that bar stand for?
pages.why: A bar is a pressure times a change in volume: 256 kPa across 0.15 − 0.1 = 0.05 m³ gives 256 × 0.05 = 12.8 kJ, the bar’s area. 256 × 0.125 = 32 multiplies by where the middle is, a volume, not the bar’s width. 256 on its own is a pressure, not work.

pages.name: Where the rule comes from
pages.text: Where does an exact answer come from? Along `pV² = 4` the pressure is `4 ÷ V²`, also written `4 × V⁻²`, because a power below zero means one over. The reverse power rule adds one to the power, giving −1, and divides by it: `4 × V⁻¹ ÷ (1 − 2)`. Differentiate that and `4 × V⁻²` comes back, so it is right. And `4 × V⁻¹` is just `pV` at each end, 40 and 20, the dashed rectangles. Put in the end, take away the start: (20 − 40) ÷ (1 − 2) = 20 kJ, the bars’ total.

pages.alt: pV squared equals 4: the exact area from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.2 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 20.00 kJ. p equals 4 divided by V squared equals 4 times V to the power minus 2: a minus power is one over. Reverse rule: power minus 2 plus 1, so 4 times V to the power minus 1 divided by (1 minus 2). Check: differentiate it and 4 times V to the power minus 2 comes back. 4 times V to the power minus 1 is pV: 40 at the start, 20 at the end. Area: (20 minus 40) divided by (1 minus 2) equals 20 kJ

pages.name: The rule
pages.text: Any `n` goes the same way. `p = C × V⁻ⁿ`, the reverse power rule gives `C × V¹⁻ⁿ ÷ (1 − n)`, and `C × V¹⁻ⁿ` is `pV` at each end. Turn both subtractions round and the work is `(p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1)`, with 1 the start and 2 the end. Here that is (40 − 20) ÷ (2 − 1) = 20 kJ, just where the bars settle. Slide `n` and the end volume: a hundred bars and the rule agree to 0.01 kJ every time. `n` = 1 is the one value the rule cannot take, as it would divide by 0.
pages.alt: pV to the power n equals C, from 400 kPa at 0.1 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.2 cubic metres. Work done by the gas, by 100 bars: 20.00 kJ. Start: p 1V 1 equals 400 times 0.1 equals 40. End: p 2 equals 100 kPa, so p 2V 2 equals 20. Rule: (40 minus 20) divided by (2 minus 1) equals 20 kJ. 100 bars: 20.00 kJ, within 0.01 kJ

pages.name: Using the rule
pages.task: Gas at 800 kPa in 0.1 m³ expands to 0.4 m³ along `pV¹·⁵ = C`, an example. `C` = 800 × 0.1¹·⁵ = 25.30 and 0.4¹·⁵ = 0.253, so at the end the pressure is 25.30 ÷ 0.253 = 100 kPa. How much work does the gas do?
pages.why: Start: 800 × 0.1 = 80; end: 100 × 0.4 = 40. The rule divides their difference by n − 1: (80 − 40) ÷ (1.5 − 1) = 40 ÷ 0.5 = 80 kJ. 40 kJ stops before dividing; 40 ÷ 1.5 = 26.7 kJ divides by n instead of n − 1. Both are much less than the area under the curve.
pages.alt: pV to the power 1.5 equals C, from 0.1 to 0.4 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.4 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 80 kJ. p 1V 1 equals 80, p 2V 2 equals 40. (80 minus 40) divided by (1.5 minus 1) equals 80 kJ

pages.name: Run it backwards
pages.text: Run it backwards and the piston squeezes the gas from 0.2 m³ at 100 kPa back to 0.1 m³ at 400 kPa. The curve is the same, still above the axis, but each bar’s width, the change in volume, is now minus, so each bar counts as minus: hatched. The rule, with 1 the start, gives (100 × 0.2 − 400 × 0.1) ÷ 1 = −20 kJ. Work done by the gas is positive for expansion and negative for compression: here the piston does 20 kJ of work on the gas. Flip the switch to run it either way.

pages.name: A squeeze
pages.task: The piston squeezes gas at 100 kPa in 0.4 m³ down to 0.1 m³ along `pV¹·⁵ = C`, an example, and it ends at 800 kPa. How much work does the gas do?
pages.why: With 1 the start: 100 × 0.4 = 40 and 800 × 0.1 = 80, so the rule gives (40 − 80) ÷ (1.5 − 1) = −40 ÷ 0.5 = −80 kJ. The volume shrinks, so every bar’s width is minus and the gas’s work is minus: the piston does 80 kJ of work on it. 80 kJ counts the squeeze as plus; −40 kJ forgets to divide by n − 1.
pages.alt: pV to the power 1.5 equals C, squeezed from 0.4 to 0.1 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.1 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: minus 80 kJ. p 1V 1 equals 40, p 2V 2 equals 80. (40 minus 80) divided by (1.5 minus 1) equals minus 80 kJ

pages.name: Mean effective pressure
pages.text: Last, lay a rectangle over the curve with the same area and the same width. Its height is its area divided by its length along the volume axis: 20 kJ ÷ 0.1 m³ = 200 kPa, the steady pressure that would do the same work. That is the idea behind the [[mean effective pressure]], which the marine syllabuses ask you to define and to find from an indicator card. It is not the average of the end pressures, 250 kPa: the curve spends most of its width below that.

pages.name: Its mean pressure
pages.task: The expansion from 800 kPa in 0.1 m³ to 100 kPa in 0.4 m³ did 80 kJ of work. What is its mean effective pressure?
pages.why: Spread the work over the change in volume, 0.4 − 0.1 = 0.3 m³: 80 ÷ 0.3 = 267 kPa, the height of a rectangle with the same area and the same width. (800 + 100) ÷ 2 = 450 kPa, the ends’ average, is too high: the curve drops fast and spends most of its width low. 80 ÷ 0.4 = 200 kPa spreads the work over the whole volume, not the change.
pages.alt: pV to the power 1.5 equals C: 80 kJ from 0.1 to 0.4 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.4 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 80 kJ. Change in volume: 0.4 minus 0.1 equals 0.3 cubic metres. 80 divided by 0.3 equals 267 kPa, the same area

pages.name: A big expansion
pages.task: Gas at 2700 kPa in 0.02 m³ expands along `pV¹·⁵ = C` to 0.18 m³, where it is at 100 kPa, an example. How much work does the gas do?
pages.why: Start: 2700 × 0.02 = 54; end: 100 × 0.18 = 18. The work done by the gas is (54 − 18) ÷ (1.5 − 1) = 36 ÷ 0.5 = 72 kJ, plus, as it expands. −72 kJ is the form some books give, (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁) ÷ (n − 1), the work done on the gas. 36 ÷ 1.5 = 24 kJ divides by n instead of n − 1.
pages.alt: pV to the power 1.5 equals C, from 0.02 to 0.18 cubic metres. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.18 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 72 kJ. p 1V 1 equals 54, p 2V 2 equals 18. (54 minus 18) divided by (1.5 minus 1) equals 72 kJ

pages.name: Flat, then falling
pages.task: Gas at a steady 500 kPa, an example, pushes the piston from 0.02 to 0.06 m³, then expands along `pV² = C` to 0.12 m³. How much work does it do in all?
pages.why: Add the two parts. The flat part is 500 × 0.04 = 20 kJ. On the curve, `C` = 500 × 0.06² = 1.8, so at 0.12 m³ the pressure is 1.8 ÷ 0.12² = 125 kPa, and the rule gives (500 × 0.06 − 125 × 0.12) ÷ (2 − 1) = (30 − 15) ÷ 1 = 15 kJ. In all, 20 + 15 = 35 kJ. 15 kJ leaves out the flat part; 500 × 0.06 = 30 is the pressure times the volume at the corner, not an area under the path.
pages.alt: A steady 500 kPa, then pV squared equals C. A cylinder whose piston sits at 0.12 cubic metres. Work done by the gas: 35 kJ. Flat part: 500 times 0.04 equals 20 kJ. Curved part: (30 minus 15) divided by 1 equals 15 kJ. 20 plus 15 equals 35 kJ
